The introduction opens on a puzzling scenario (jacket ships before the socks) and states the claim; no dictionary opening, throat-clearing or 'in today's world' pattern.
The conclusion opens on a callback with the answer, then sorts take-aways by how settled they are and turns them into questions; it is not a bare restatement of the sections.

What to Take Away ¶1 joins the witnesses (payment provider, warehouse per parcel, carrier, returns portal) into one answer and names how the home is chosen; the author's synthesis and the nine questions turn it into action (name the order's home, its number family, per-shipment status). The spec's line that Kestrel & Pine's remedy was 'the decision first and the purchase second' is not said explicitly; not enough to fail.

'Go back to the order of the opening, whose jacket shipped before the socks' says what it should have read, what the customer should have been told and which system should hold it, as the callback declares.

The intro-only reader predicted all roadmap promises in order (Three-Status Order, record and number, states and the computed status, edits/holds/cancellations, routing and splits, one home and which system, the OMS, four homes by trade-off and stage, the chosen design replayed, failures) and the evidence (the Kestrel & Pine case and platform/OMS vendor documentation). It was unsure how far Eva runs through the chapter (ruled under flow).

Answer matches expected: 'Partially delivered: 1 of 2 parcels' and 'ships in two parcels'; goods status per shipment with the least-advanced-shipment rule; the design had one status string, and no single home held the order across platform, WMS and ERP.

Answer matches expected: yes, two of four conditions hold (two channels, two warehouses); an OMS rather than the ERP because the hub must route between warehouses and answer consumers' parcel questions, which a batch finance system cannot. Nothing in the answer ties the decision to revenue.

Answer matches expected: a shipped order cannot be canceled; it becomes a return (label, receipt, inspection, refund on receipt), a compensation coordinated by the order's home; edits/cancellations are checked against the goods state.
